paragraphs.heading: Coast, shore and beach
paragraphs.text: A coast is the land beside the sea, or the boundary line between the land and the ocean or a lake. The topography of the landscape around a coast influences it, and so does erosion by water, such as the erosion waves cause. The geological makeup of the rock and soil dictates what type of shore is created. Physical oceanography treats a shore as the wider fringe that the body of water has geologically modified, in the past and the present. The beach lies at the edge of the shore and includes the intertidal zone where there is one.

paragraphs.heading: What waves do
paragraphs.text: Waves erode the coastline as they break on shore and release their energy. A larger wave releases more energy and moves more sediment. The form of the coast matters as well. Where shores are longer, waves have more room to disperse their energy. Where a coast has cliffs and short shore faces, there is little room for that energy to be dispersed.

paragraphs.heading: What tides do
paragraphs.text: Tides often set the range over which sediment is laid down or eroded. Where the tidal range is high, waves can reach farther up the shore. Where the tidal range is lower, deposition happens over a smaller interval of elevation. The size and shape of the coastline influence the tidal range. Tides do not typically cause erosion by themselves. Tidal bores can erode, however, as their waves surge from the ocean up river estuaries.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting coasts by their tides
paragraphs.text: Geologists classify coasts by tidal range. Macrotidal coasts have a tidal range greater than 4 m, mesotidal coasts a range of 2 to 4 m, and microtidal coasts a range of less than 2 m. Macrotidal coasts lack barrier islands and lagoons. They are characterized by funnel-shaped estuaries, which contain sand ridges aligned with the tidal currents. On mesotidal and microtidal coasts, wave action is much more important in determining the bedforms of deposited sediment than it is on macrotidal coasts.

paragraphs.heading: Life sorted by exposure
paragraphs.text: Different shores hold different living communities. In areas protected from waves, coasts harbor salt marshes, mangroves and seagrasses. Rocky shores are usually found along exposed coasts, and they give a home to a wide range of sessile animals, such as mussels, starfish and barnacles, and to various kinds of seaweeds. Along tropical coasts where the water is clear and poor in nutrients, coral reefs often occur at depths of 1–50 m.

paragraphs.heading: A line that cannot be pinned down
paragraphs.text: Earth has about 620,000 km of coastline. Coasts are constantly changing, so the exact perimeter of a coastline cannot be determined. That difficulty of measurement has a name: the coastline paradox.
